Choosing a kettle for a small kitchen

Size

A kettle is the most used appliance in most kitchens and the least considered. In a small kitchen the first question is how much water you actually boil at once. A litre is enough for four mugs of tea, and a kettle that holds a litre and a half is already more than most households fill. Larger kettles take up counter space, take longer to boil when they are full, and tempt people into heating water they then pour away.

Speed and power

Boiling time depends on the heating element and on how much water is in the kettle, not on the brand. A three kilowatt element brings a litre to the boil in a little over two minutes; a two kilowatt element takes nearly a minute longer. If your kitchen shares a circuit with other heavy appliances, the slower kettle is the kinder choice. Variable temperature models are worth the extra money if you drink green tea or make coffee by hand, because both are better with water well below boiling.

Noise and materials

Stainless steel kettles are quiet and last for years but show every fingerprint. Glass kettles let you see the water and the scale, which some people like and some people cannot stand. Plastic is the cheapest and the lightest and also the one most likely to smell of itself for the first week. Whatever the material, a kettle with a wide lid is easier to descale, and descaling once a month is what keeps the boil fast.
